# DebugBench Data Audit Report (plan_005)

## 1. Data Attrition: 1414 → 1024 (-390, 27.6%)

### Stage 1: Test Building (1414 → 1222, -192)
| Reason | Count | % of 1414 |
|--------|-------|-----------|
| ok (usable) | 1222 | 86.4% |
| skip_complex (TreeNode/ListNode etc.) | 160 | 11.3% |
| skip_parse_fail (can't parse I/O) | 26 | 1.8% |
| skip_nondeterministic | 6 | 0.4% |

### Stage 2: Validation (1222 → 1024, -198)
Correct solution fails generated test cases. By bug category:
| Category | Filtered |
|----------|----------|
| multiple error | ~121 |
| reference error | ~23 |
| syntax error | ~21 |
| logic error | ~16 |

Note: category counts approximate (slug+subtype dedup); total confirmed 198 by line count.

### Pipeline
```
debugbench_python.jsonl (1414)
  → debugbench_test_builder.py → test_cases.jsonl (1222)
  → debugbench_validate_tests.py → test_cases_validated.jsonl (1024)
  → debugbench_collect_traces.py → raw_traces.jsonl (2048 = 1024×2)
  → debugbench_format_data.py → 3 conditions × (1622 train + 426 test)
```

## 2. VOTA Condition: MISSING

`debugbench_format_data.py` only generates 3 conditions: no_trace, exception_only, full_trace.
No VOTA formatting path was implemented for DebugBench.

Files present:
- ✅ debugbench_no_trace_{train,test}.jsonl
- ✅ debugbench_exception_only_{train,test}.jsonl
- ✅ debugbench_full_trace_{train,test}.jsonl
- ❌ debugbench_vota_{train,test}.jsonl — does not exist

## 3. Exception_only Theoretical Ceiling: 71.1%

### Test set composition (426 samples)
| | Pass | Fail | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Has exception data | 0 | 84 | 84 |
| No exception data | 219 | 123 | 342 |
| Total | 219 | 207 | 426 |

- 59.4% of fail samples have NO exception → logic errors invisible to exception_only
- All pass samples have no exception → "no exception" is ambiguous signal
- **Theoretical ceiling**: 303/426 = **71.1%** (all pass + all fail-with-exception correct)
- Majority baseline: 51.4% (pass)

### DebugBench "logic error" exception detail
- 134 buggy fail samples labeled "logic error"
- 121/134 (90.3%) actually DO produce exception events (downstream failures)
- Only 13/134 (9.7%) are truly exception-free logic errors

## 4. Full_trace Token Length (Qwen tokenizer, +32 chat overhead)

| Metric | full_trace | exception_only | no_trace |
|--------|------------|----------------|----------|
| Mean | 1508.2 | 372.4 | 273.9 |
| Median | 2048 | 293 | 226 |
| Max | 2048 | 1859 | 1849 |
| >2048 | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) | 0 (0%) |
| >1024 | 1424 (69.5%) | — | — |

- **68.9% of full_trace samples are truncated** (1412/2048 hit 2048-token cap)
- Median at 2048 = majority of samples lose trace information
- Truncation is one-directional: only full_trace affected, exception_only and no_trace well within limits

## 5. Raw Trace Quality

| Code type | Pass | Fail | Total |
|-----------|------|------|-------|
| correct | 1016 | 8 | 1024 |
| buggy | 26 | 998 | 1024 |

- 8 correct solutions fail tests (0.8%) — test case edge cases
- 26 buggy solutions pass tests (2.5%) — bugs not triggered by generated tests
- 625/2048 (30.5%) have empty trace_raw

## 6. Registry Status

No plan_005 experiments registered. Only data preparation complete; no training has been run on DebugBench data.

# DeepSeek VOTA Seed42 实验分析

## 实验配置
- Model: deepseek-ai/deepseek-coder-6.7b-instruct
- Condition: vota
- Data: 4720 train / 1190 test
- Seed: 42
- Training: 3 epochs, 444 steps, ~2h12m on cuda:0

## 核心指标

| Metric | Value | 95% CI |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Accuracy | 84.45% | [82.60%, 86.39%] |
| Majority baseline | 71.51% | [69.16%, 73.87%] |
| Lift | +12.94pp | [+11.09pp, +14.87pp] |

### Per-class metrics

| Class | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|-------|-----------|--------|-----|
| pass | 0.821 [0.800, 0.843] | 1.000 [1.000, 1.000] | 0.902 [0.889, 0.915] |
| fail | 1.000 [1.000, 1.000] | 0.454 [0.405, 0.505] | 0.625 [0.576, 0.671] |

Bootstrap: 1000 resamples

## 训练 Loss 曲线

**Train loss（第一个 epoch 采样）：**
- epoch 0.07: 0.4668 → epoch 0.27: 0.1057 → epoch 0.95: 0.0522
- 快速收敛，0.3 epoch 内 loss 从 0.47 降到 0.09

**Eval loss & classification accuracy by epoch：**
| Epoch | Eval Loss | Eval Mean Token Acc | Verdict Accuracy | Fail Recall |
|-------|-----------|---------------------|-----------------|-------------|
| 1.0 | 0.0679 | 0.9802 | 78.15% | 23.3% |
| 2.0 | 0.0950 | 0.9794 | — | — |
| 3.0 | 0.1121 | 0.9791 | 84.45% | 45.4% |

**eval_loss 与 classification accuracy 解耦**：eval_loss 单调递增 (+65%) 但 verdict accuracy 从 78.15% 提升到 84.45% (+6.3pp)，fail recall 从 23.3% 提升到 45.4% (+22.1pp)。continued training 改善了分类能力（尤其是 fail 识别），eval_loss 上升反映 token-level calibration 退化而非分类能力下降。eval_loss 不是 verdict task 的可靠 checkpoint selection criterion。

### Epoch-level Classification Performance
| Epoch | Eval Loss | Accuracy | Fail Recall | Fail Precision |
|-------|-----------|----------|-------------|----------------|
| 1 | 0.0679 | 78.15% | 23.3% | — |
| 3 (final) | 0.1121 | 84.45% | 45.4% | 100% |

Continued training improves verdict classification (+6.3pp accuracy, +22.1pp fail recall) despite increasing eval_loss. This validates using the final checkpoint rather than the lowest-loss checkpoint for verdict classification.

## Within-Model 对比（DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B）

| Condition | Accuracy | 95% CI |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| DeepSeek no_trace | 73.4% | [70.8%, 75.7%] |
| **DeepSeek VOTA** | **84.5%** | **[82.6%, 86.4%]** |
| **Within-model lift** | **+11.09pp** | CI 不重叠，显著 |

- deepseek_no_trace conclusion = **negative**（lift +1.85pp over majority, CI [-0.93, +4.63] 跨 0，不显著）
- DeepSeek VOTA within-model lift: 84.45% − 73.36% = **+11.09pp**，统计显著

### Cross-Model Comparison (Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B vs DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B)

| Condition | Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B | DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B | Δ |
|-----------|-------------------|---------------------|---|
| no_trace | 75.1% [72.8, 77.5] | 73.4% [70.8, 75.7] | −1.7pp（CI 重叠，不显著）|
| VOTA | 99.2% [98.6, 99.7] | 84.5% [82.6, 86.4] | −14.7pp（显著）|
| VOTA within-model lift | +24.0pp | +11.1pp | — |

**核心发现**：两模型 no_trace 基线接近（Δ = −1.7pp，不显著）→ VOTA 效果差距 (−14.7pp) 完全来自 trace 利用效率差异，而非基础代码理解能力差距。

## 关键发现

1. **Pass 偏向严重**：模型对 pass 有 100% recall 但对 fail 只有 45.4% recall，说明模型倾向于预测 pass。Fail precision 为 1.0 表示当模型预测 fail 时总是对的，但它漏掉了超过一半的 fail 样本。
2. **eval_loss 与 verdict accuracy 解耦**：eval loss 从 epoch 1 的 0.068 增加到 epoch 3 的 0.112 (+65%)，但 verdict accuracy 从 78.15% 提升到 84.45% (+6.3pp)，fail recall 从 23.3% 提升到 45.4% (+22.1pp)。eval_loss 上升反映 token-level calibration 退化，不是分类能力下降。这验证了 revert load_best_model_at_end 的决策正确性——用 eval_loss 选 checkpoint 会选到分类能力更差的 epoch 1。
3. **VOTA 对 DeepSeek 有效但 trace 利用效率远低于 Qwen**：DeepSeek VOTA within-model lift +11.09pp（vs DeepSeek no_trace 73.4%），而 Qwen VOTA lift +24.0pp。两模型 no_trace 基线接近（Δ=1.7pp，不显著），VOTA 效果差距完全来自 trace 利用效率差异。

## 结论

**Success** — accuracy 84.5% 显著高于 DeepSeek no_trace baseline 73.4%（within-model lift +11.09pp，95% CI 不重叠），VOTA 条件对 DeepSeek 模型同样有效。但 within-model lift (+11.1pp) 远低于 Qwen (+24.0pp)，且两模型 no_trace 基线接近（Δ=1.7pp，不显著），说明 trace 利用效率是跨模型效果差异的主因。

\section{Experiments}

We evaluate our trace preprocessing pipeline across two research questions:
(1)~Do Tier~1 exception signals generalize across models of different capability?
(2)~What is the relative contribution of each trace component to verdict prediction accuracy?
All experiments use our trace--verdict dataset (\S\ref{sec:dataset}) with $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals unless stated otherwise.
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all cross-condition differences reported below are significant at $p{<}0.0001$ unless noted otherwise.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

To test whether exception-based trace compression transfers across model families, we compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions: \texttt{exception\_only} (Tier~1 exception events), VOTA (exception + assertion-point + loop compression), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete execution trace), and \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-2.5-7B} & \textbf{DeepSeek-6.7B} & \textbf{Gap} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}\% & 99.33\%$^\dag$ & 0.50pp \\
VOTA & 99.41\% & 84.45\% & 14.96pp \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & 99.41\%$^\S$ & --- & --- \\
full\_trace & 81.76\% & N/A$^\ddag$ & --- \\
no\_trace & 75.13\% & 73.36\% & 1.77pp \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & 71.51\% & 71.51\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cross-model accuracy ($N{=}1{,}190$). Qwen CIs: exception\_only [99.58, 100.00], VOTA [98.82, 99.83], full\_trace [79.70, 83.90], no\_trace [72.77, 77.48]; DeepSeek CIs: VOTA [82.60, 86.40], no\_trace [70.80, 75.70]. $^\dag$DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} 3-seed results: 99.33\% (seeds 42, 456; CI [98.82, 99.75]) and 91.09\% (seed 123; CI [89.40, 92.60]); seed 123 is a LoRA initialization outlier (fail recall = 70.5\% vs.\ 100\%). $^\S$VOTA\_no\_ae evaluated on Qwen only; CI [98.90, 99.80]. $^\ddag$DeepSeek full\_trace was invalidated because the DeepSeek tokenizer produced sequences exceeding 2{,}048 tokens, causing the verdict label to be truncated during training; the model consequently failed to learn the classification task.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reveals a striking asymmetry.
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, Qwen achieves 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 across three seeds, while DeepSeek shows a bimodal pattern: seeds 42 and 456 both achieve 99.33\% (gap = 0.50pp), while seed 123 yields 91.09\% (gap = 8.74pp), attributable to suboptimal LoRA initialization (fail recall = 70.5\% vs.\ 100\% for other seeds).
Even the outlier seed outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp, confirming exception events as the most effective component across models.
Under VOTA, the gap widens to 14.96pp: DeepSeek drops to 84.45\% while Qwen remains at 99.41\%.
Post-hoc tokenizer analysis reveals a confound: measured on the training set using each model's tokenizer, the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}759 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}908 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
Unlike the DeepSeek \texttt{full\_trace} condition (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}, $^\ddag$), where right-truncation removed the verdict label entirely, the VOTA training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content (input), so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the vast majority of the dataset.
The 14.96pp gap thus reflects both model capability differences and training-time trace truncation; the two factors cannot be disentangled in the current design.
In contrast, the \texttt{exception\_only} condition is unaffected by truncation because exception-based inputs are short enough to fit within the context window for both tokenizers, making its cross-model comparison clean.
Per-class analysis (Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}) reveals the mechanism: DeepSeek VOTA achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}---in contrast to Qwen VOTA, which achieves 100\% fail recall.

The \texttt{no\_trace} baseline confirms that source code alone provides limited signal (75.13\% for Qwen, 73.36\% for DeepSeek), only marginally above majority-class guessing (71.51\%).

Seed robustness diverges sharply across models.
Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical accuracy of 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$, exactly two errors each).
DeepSeek shows a bimodal pattern ($n{=}3$): seeds 42 and 456 both achieve 99.33\% (8 errors each, fail recall = 100\%), while seed 123 yields 91.09\% (fail recall = 70.5\%), consistent with LoRA initialization sensitivity on the smaller model.
Because the \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% duplicate inputs (607 unique out of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), the reported CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials.
Under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's two errors yield 99.67\% accuracy (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]), confirming that the result is robust to the effective sample size.

\subsection{Component Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}

We decompose the VOTA pipeline into individual components on Qwen-2.5-7B (seed=42).
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} arranges conditions into a two-tier hierarchy: Tier~1 signals (\texttt{ae\_only}, \texttt{exception\_only}) that individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy, and Tier~2 signals (\texttt{loop\_only}) that provide moderate improvement over the no-trace baseline.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & assertion-point & \textbf{99.92} & [99.75, 100.00] & 1 \\
exception\_only & exception events & 99.83 & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.41 & [98.82, 99.83] & --- \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
loop\_only & loop compression & 85.63 & [83.53, 87.56] & 2 \\
full\_trace & complete trace & 81.76 & [79.70, 83.90] & --- \\
no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). Tier~1 signals individually achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

Two findings stand out.
First, the Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{ae\_only} (99.92\%) and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) are not distinguishable ($p{=}0.80$, paired bootstrap, $B{=}10{,}000$), and both exceed VOTA (99.41\%, $p{=}0.01$ for \texttt{exception\_only} vs.\ VOTA, paired bootstrap).
This implies that combining signals in VOTA introduces minor noise rather than complementary information.
Second, removing assertion points from VOTA has no effect (VOTA\_no\_ae = VOTA = 99.41\%), confirming that within the VOTA mixture, exception events dominate the prediction signal.

Tier~2 signal \texttt{loop\_only} (85.63\%) improves over \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%) by 10.50pp ($p{<}0.0001$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[{+}8.24, {+}12.86]$), showing that loop compression captures some execution semantics, but far less than exception events.

\subsection{Information Density Decomposition}
\label{sec:density}

The gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) and VOTA (99.41\%) is 17.65pp.
We decompose this gap into two mechanisms by introducing an intermediate condition, \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}, which retains the complete trace as input but computes loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace tokens during training.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
\midrule
full\_trace & 81.76 & --- & --- \\
label\_only & 86.22 & +4.46pp & 26\% \\
VOTA & 99.41 & +17.65pp & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Information density decomposition. The full\_trace$\to$VOTA gap decomposes into gradient dilution (26\%, addressed by masking trace tokens from the loss) and information overload (74\%, addressed by removing irrelevant trace lines via VOTA compression).}
\label{tab:density}
\end{table}

As shown in Table~\ref{tab:density}, the decomposition attributes 26\% of the gap (+4.46pp, $p{<}0.0001$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[{+}2.35, {+}6.55]$) to \emph{gradient dilution}---the training signal is diluted across trace tokens that do not contribute to verdict prediction---and 74\% (+13.19pp) to \emph{information overload}---the model must process trace lines irrelevant to the fault at inference time.
This two-factor decomposition is consistent across models: the VOTA cross-model gap (14.96pp, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is confounded by training-time trace truncation on DeepSeek (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}), which amplifies information overload by removing diagnostic trace content from the majority of training samples.

\subsection{Calibration Analysis}
\label{sec:calibration}

Beyond accuracy, we evaluate whether trace conditions affect prediction calibration, motivated by recent findings that code LLM confidence is often poorly calibrated \citep{spiess2025calibration}.
Figure~\ref{fig:calibration} shows reliability diagrams for four conditions on Qwen-2.5-7B.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{ECE $\downarrow$} & \textbf{Brier $\downarrow$} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & \textbf{0.0004} & \textbf{0.0008} \\
exception\_only & 0.003 & 0.0013 \\
VOTA & 0.005 & 0.005 \\
full\_trace & 0.096 & 0.144 \\
no\_trace & 0.171 & 0.197 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Calibration metrics on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). ECE = expected calibration error; Brier = Brier score. Lower is better for both.}
\label{tab:calibration}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:calibration} shows that calibration quality mirrors the Tier~1/2 hierarchy.
Tier~1 conditions (\texttt{ae\_only}: ECE=0.0004; \texttt{exception\_only}: ECE=0.003) produce near-perfectly calibrated predictions, while \texttt{full\_trace} (ECE=0.096) and \texttt{no\_trace} (ECE=0.171) exhibit substantial miscalibration.
VOTA (ECE=0.005) is well-calibrated but slightly worse than either Tier~1 component alone, reinforcing the pattern that combining trace signals dilutes rather than improves the prediction signal.

The Brier scores tell a consistent story: \texttt{ae\_only} (0.0008) and \texttt{exception\_only} (0.0013) achieve near-zero scores, while \texttt{no\_trace} (0.197) indicates substantial miscalibration.

Figure~\ref{fig:cross_model_gap} visualizes the cross-model gap pattern, showing that exception-based conditions maintain tight cross-model agreement while VOTA and lower-tier conditions diverge.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig2_calibration}
\caption{Reliability diagrams for four trace conditions on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$, seed=42). The Tier~1 condition (\texttt{exception\_only}) clusters near the diagonal (well-calibrated), while \texttt{full\_trace} and \texttt{no\_trace} exhibit systematic overconfidence.}
\label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Cross-model accuracy gap (Qwen $-$ DeepSeek) across trace conditions. Exception-based signals transfer across models (0.50pp gap), while VOTA is model-dependent (14.96pp gap).}
\label{fig:cross_model_gap}
\end{figure}

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces---line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior---have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models.
Recent work has explored trace-augmented training for code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile}, execution-aware pretraining \citep{ding2024traced}, trace-based code understanding \citep{wang2025dcsh}, and self-training on trace chain-of-thought \citep{ni2024next}.
Yet a fundamental question remains open: \emph{which components of an execution trace actually matter?}

\citet{wang2025dcsh} found that no single trace representation consistently outperforms others on generation-oriented tasks, concluding that the utility of execution traces is task- and format-dependent.
However, their study focused on code generation and repair---tasks that require the model to simulate or reconstruct execution semantics.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---is a fundamentally different task type: it is a fault detection problem, not a generation problem.
Whether the same trace components matter for fault detection as for generation is unknown.

We present the first systematic study of what trace components drive verdict prediction performance.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} with model-generated solutions and execution traces, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components and evaluate each in isolation across two models: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct.

Our results reveal a striking finding: \textbf{exception events alone achieve near-perfect verdict prediction on Qwen (99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00, 3 seeds) and are the most effective component on DeepSeek, with 2/3 seeds matching Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the remaining seed (91.09\%) reflects LoRA initialization sensitivity rather than a signal limitation.}
Even the DeepSeek outlier seed (91.09\%) outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) and no-trace (73.36\%) by wide margins, confirming exception events as the dominant trace component across models.
In contrast, the full VOTA representation---which combines exception events with assertion-point and loop information---degrades by 14.96pp on DeepSeek.
Post-hoc analysis reveals the mechanism: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing 91.7\% of VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window; the training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content, so the model trains on incomplete diagnostic information.

These results reframe verdict prediction as fault detection: the minimal sufficient signal is the exception event, a compact structured diagnostic moment that both models can interpret without deep trace reasoning.
We further decompose the gap between full trace and VOTA into two mechanisms---\emph{gradient dilution} (26\% of the gap) and \emph{information overload} (74\%)---showing that the primary bottleneck is not training signal quality but the presence of irrelevant trace content.

We note that the finding that exception events dominate verdict prediction is not itself surprising---exceptions are, by definition, fault indicators.
The novelty lies in three less obvious results: (1)~adding more trace information actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}), (2)~we quantify \emph{why} through a 26/74 gradient-dilution/information-overload decomposition, and (3)~the VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation: the DeepSeek tokenizer causes the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}), truncating diagnostic trace content while preserving the verdict label.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exception signal transfer}: We show that exception events alone achieve 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 on Qwen (3 seeds) and 99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds, with one outlier at 91.09\% from LoRA initialization sensitivity; even the outlier exceeds VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
\item \textbf{Information density decomposition}: We decompose the full-trace-to-VOTA gap into gradient dilution (26\%) and information overload (74\%), identifying the primary bottleneck for trace-based prediction (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Component ablation reveals that Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach only 85.6\% (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Discussion}
2	
3	\subsection{Why Exception Events Dominate}
4	
5	Verdict prediction is fundamentally a fault detection task: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
6	Exception events are the most explicit signal of such deviation---structured diagnostic moments that encode the nature and location of a fault.
7	Unlike loop compressions or assertion-point values, which require the model to integrate information across multiple trace elements, exception events provide a self-contained verdict cue.
8	This explains why \texttt{exception\_only} matches or exceeds VOTA: adding non-exception trace components dilutes the model's attention on the diagnostic signal rather than providing complementary information.
9	
10	We acknowledge that exception-based verdict prediction is, at its core, fault indicator presence detection: the model learns to map the presence or absence of a structured error message to a binary label, which is close to trivially solvable for any instruction-tuned LLM.
11	The Tier~1 accuracy of ${\geq}$99.8\% is therefore unsurprising in isolation.
12	The contribution of this finding lies not in demonstrating that a strong signal yields high accuracy, but in two less obvious results: (a)~adding more trace information---loop compressions, assertion-point values---actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), quantifying an information density dilution effect that has not been previously measured; and (b)~this dilution is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation on DeepSeek: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}); the verdict label is preserved, but the trace content is truncated, depriving the model of diagnostic information and contributing to the collapse of DeepSeek VOTA fail recall to 45.43\% (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) while Qwen maintains 100\%.
13	
14	\subsection{Simplicity as Relative Robustness}
15	
16	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
17	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity---a fixed-format error message---ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
18	Two of three DeepSeek seeds match Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the outlier (seed 123, 91.09\%) is attributable to LoRA initialization landing in a suboptimal basin (fail recall = 70.5\%), not to a failure of the exception signal itself---even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
19	The VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by two factors: (1)~tokenizer efficiency---the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}759 tokens per VOTA sample versus Qwen's 1{,}908, causing 91.7\% of training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window, truncating trace content while preserving the verdict label---and (2)~base model capability differences, consistent with findings that SFT generalization depends on pretrain quality \citep{yang2024generalization}.
20	The two factors cannot be disentangled in the current experimental design.
21	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely by keeping inputs short (median 314 tokens), making its cross-model comparison clean and the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
22	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal; for smaller models, training stability (multi-seed selection, warmup schedules) is a secondary but addressable concern.
23	
24	\subsection{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
25	
26	The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results reveal two instructive training dynamics.
27	First, epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in 2/3 seeds: seed 42 peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), seed 123 degrades from 91.43\% to 91.09\% ($-$0.34pp), while seed 456 shows no epoch degradation (99.33\% at both epoch~1 and epoch~3).
28	Early stopping may yield marginal gains for some seeds, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp) compared to the seed effect (8.24pp between seeds 42 and 123).
29	
30	Second, seeds 123 and 456 converge to nearly identical final training losses (0.122 and 0.123 respectively), yet their accuracies differ by 8.24pp (91.09\% vs.\ 99.33\%).
31	The critical difference lies in fail recall: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 100\%, while seed 123 achieves only 70.5\%---the LoRA initialization in seed 123 fails to learn the exception$\to$fail mapping for a substantial fraction of failing samples, even though the per-token loss appears converged.
32	This demonstrates that token-level training loss can mask fundamental differences in sample-level classification ability, suggesting a parallel to the eval-loss/accuracy decoupling observed in DeepSeek VOTA (where eval loss rose 65\% from epoch 1 to 3 while accuracy improved by 6.3pp) at the training phase.
33	The practical recommendation is twofold: (1)~use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training or evaluation loss, and (2)~for deployment on smaller models, train multiple seeds and select the best, as a single run may not reliably converge to the correct classification boundary.
34	
35	The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, but is consistent with a performance limit associated with the high trace truncation rate (\S\ref{sec:cross_model})---the model progressively extracts signal from samples with intact trace content but cannot fully compensate for the information loss in the truncated majority.
36	The 84.45\% accuracy reflects a combination of trace information loss and model capability constraints.
37	
38	\subsection{Error Analysis}
39	\label{sec:error_analysis}
40	
41	Seed robustness testing revealed that the two errors made by \texttt{exception\_only} (accuracy = 99.83\%, 2/1190 incorrect) are \emph{identical across all three seeds} (42, 123, 456).
42	Both errors are false negatives on samples involving the \texttt{check\_dict\_case} function (sample IDs 901 and 905): the ground truth is \texttt{pass}, but the model predicts \texttt{fail}.
43	This 100\% error overlap ($\sigma{=}0$) across seeds demonstrates that these are not stochastic training artifacts but \emph{irreducible samples} at the boundary of what exception-based trace signals can resolve.
44	
45	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95) uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
46	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
47	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
48	This is not a model failure but a \emph{representation ceiling}: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
49	The 99.83\% accuracy is therefore a deterministic upper bound for this trace representation on this dataset, not an indication of insufficient model capacity.
50	
51	\subsection{Limitations}
52	
53	Our study has several limitations.
54	First, all experiments use a single dataset (591 problems from HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized); generalization to other languages, larger codebases, or different fault types remains untested.
55	Second, we evaluate only two models at the 7B parameter scale; the relationship between model size and trace signal utility is unexplored.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why Exception Events Dominate}

Verdict prediction is fundamentally a fault detection task: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit signal of such deviation---structured diagnostic moments that encode the nature and location of a fault.
Unlike loop compressions or assertion-point values, which require the model to integrate information across multiple trace elements, exception events provide a self-contained verdict cue.
This explains why \texttt{exception\_only} matches or exceeds VOTA: adding non-exception trace components dilutes the model's attention on the diagnostic signal rather than providing complementary information.

We acknowledge that exception-based verdict prediction is, at its core, fault indicator presence detection: the model learns to map the presence or absence of a structured error message to a binary label, which is close to trivially solvable for any instruction-tuned LLM.
The Tier~1 accuracy of ${\geq}$99.8\% is therefore unsurprising in isolation.
The contribution of this finding lies not in demonstrating that a strong signal yields high accuracy, but in two less obvious results: (a)~adding more trace information---loop compressions, assertion-point values---actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), quantifying an information density dilution effect that has not been previously measured; and (b)~this dilution is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation on DeepSeek: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}); the verdict label is preserved, but the trace content is truncated, depriving the model of diagnostic information and contributing to the collapse of DeepSeek VOTA fail recall to 45.43\% (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) while Qwen maintains 100\%.

\subsection{Simplicity as Relative Robustness}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity---a fixed-format error message---ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
Two of three DeepSeek seeds match Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the outlier (seed 123, 91.09\%) is attributable to LoRA initialization landing in a suboptimal basin (fail recall = 70.5\%), not to a failure of the exception signal itself---even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
The VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by two factors: (1)~tokenizer efficiency---the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}759 tokens per VOTA sample versus Qwen's 1{,}908, causing 91.7\% of training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window, truncating trace content while preserving the verdict label---and (2)~base model capability differences, consistent with findings that SFT generalization depends on pretrain quality \citep{yang2024generalization}.
The two factors cannot be disentangled in the current experimental design.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely by keeping inputs short (median 314 tokens), making its cross-model comparison clean and the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal; for smaller models, training stability (multi-seed selection, warmup schedules) is a secondary but addressable concern.

\subsection{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results reveal two instructive training dynamics.
First, epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in 2/3 seeds: seed 42 peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), seed 123 degrades from 91.43\% to 91.09\% ($-$0.34pp), while seed 456 shows no epoch degradation (99.33\% at both epoch~1 and epoch~3).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains for some seeds, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp) compared to the seed effect (8.24pp between seeds 42 and 123).

Second, seeds 123 and 456 converge to nearly identical final training losses (0.122 and 0.123 respectively), yet their accuracies differ by 8.24pp (91.09\% vs.\ 99.33\%).
The critical difference lies in fail recall: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 100\%, while seed 123 achieves only 70.5\%---the LoRA initialization in seed 123 fails to learn the exception$\to$fail mapping for a substantial fraction of failing samples, even though the per-token loss appears converged.
This demonstrates that token-level training loss can mask fundamental differences in sample-level classification ability, suggesting a parallel to the eval-loss/accuracy decoupling observed in DeepSeek VOTA (where eval loss rose 65\% from epoch 1 to 3 while accuracy improved by 6.3pp) at the training phase.
The practical recommendation is twofold: (1)~use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training or evaluation loss, and (2)~for deployment on smaller models, train multiple seeds and select the best, as a single run may not reliably converge to the correct classification boundary.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, but is consistent with a performance limit associated with the high trace truncation rate (\S\ref{sec:cross_model})---the model progressively extracts signal from samples with intact trace content but cannot fully compensate for the information loss in the truncated majority.
The 84.45\% accuracy reflects a combination of trace information loss and model capability constraints.

\subsection{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

Seed robustness testing revealed that the two errors made by \texttt{exception\_only} (accuracy = 99.83\%, 2/1190 incorrect) are \emph{identical across all three seeds} (42, 123, 456).
Both errors are false negatives on samples involving the \texttt{check\_dict\_case} function (sample IDs 901 and 905): the ground truth is \texttt{pass}, but the model predicts \texttt{fail}.
This 100\% error overlap ($\sigma{=}0$) across seeds demonstrates that these are not stochastic training artifacts but \emph{irreducible samples} at the boundary of what exception-based trace signals can resolve.

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95) uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a \emph{representation ceiling}: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
The 99.83\% accuracy is therefore a deterministic upper bound for this trace representation on this dataset, not an indication of insufficient model capacity.

\subsection{Limitations}

Our study has several limitations.
First, all experiments use a single dataset (591 problems from HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized); generalization to other languages, larger codebases, or different fault types remains untested.
Second, we evaluate only two models at the 7B parameter scale; the relationship between model size and trace signal utility is unexplored.
Third, DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} exhibits seed-dependent variance: 2/3 seeds achieve 99.33\% while seed 123 yields 91.09\% ($\sigma{=}4.76$pp, $n{=}3$), attributable to LoRA initialization sensitivity (fail recall = 70.5\% for the outlier vs.\ 100\% for others).
Qwen shows perfect seed robustness ($\sigma{=}0$, $n{=}3$).
Whether training stabilization techniques (e.g., larger warmup ratio, LoRA rank adjustment) can eliminate DeepSeek's seed sensitivity is unexplored.
Other conditions use a single seed.
Fourth, the DeepSeek \texttt{full\_trace} condition was invalidated because the DeepSeek tokenizer produced sequences exceeding 2,048 tokens, causing the verdict label to be truncated during training; the model consequently failed to learn the classification task, and we report it as N/A rather than presenting potentially misleading results.
Fifth, the candidate solutions were generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, which also serves as one of our evaluation models.
This does not affect verdict prediction---the task is to classify a \emph{given} solution as pass or fail, not to generate solutions---but we note the overlap for transparency.
Moreover, the pass/fail distribution in the dataset is determined by the generating model's coding ability; a stronger or weaker generator would yield a different class balance, potentially affecting task difficulty and the generalizability of our accuracy estimates.
Finally, our analysis is limited to verdict prediction; whether exception dominance extends to other classification tasks (vulnerability detection, clone detection) or to generation tasks (program repair) is an open question.

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.

The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ceiling: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic study of what execution trace components drive verdict prediction performance.
Through component ablation across two code LLMs, we established three findings:

\textbf{(1) Exception signal transfer.}
Exception events alone achieve 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 on Qwen (3 seeds) and 99.33\% on 2/3 DeepSeek seeds, with one outlier at 91.09\% from LoRA initialization sensitivity.

\textbf{(2) Information density decomposition.}
The 17.65pp gap between full traces and VOTA decomposes into gradient dilution (26\%, from training on irrelevant trace tokens) and information overload (74\%, from processing irrelevant trace lines at inference).
The primary bottleneck is trace content selection, not loss design.

\textbf{(3) Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy.}
Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach 85.6\%.
Combining tiers in VOTA slightly degrades performance (99.41\%), confirming that additional trace components introduce noise rather than complementary signal.

# DebugBench Exception Extraction Bug Analysis

## Bug Summary
`debugbench_format_data.py` 的 `compress_exception_only()` 丢失 62.7% fail 样本的异常信号。

## Root Cause
`compress_exception_only()` (L96) 仅调用 `compressor._extract_exceptions(trace_events)`，该方法只检查 `trace_raw` 中 `event=="exception"` 的事件。

两个问题：
1. **625/1006 fail 样本 trace_raw 为空列表**（syntax error 等在代码解析阶段就失败，无法产生 trace 事件）
2. **5/1006 fail 样本 trace 达 2000 事件上限**，异常发生在上限之后（如 RecursionError, IndexError）
3. `format_sample()` L124 的 `if trace_raw` 短路：空 trace 直接返回 "[No exception data in trace]"，不检查其他字段

但所有 1006 个 fail 样本都有 `test_results.error` 字段记录了实际异常信息。所有 1042 个 pass 样本的 `test_results.error` 为 None。

## Empty trace 分布（按 bug_category）
| Category | Total fail | Empty trace | Has exc event | Has trace no exc |
|----------|-----------|-------------|---------------|-----------------|
| syntax error | 200 | 173 (86.5%) | 27 | 0 |
| logic error | 136 | 12 (8.8%) | 121 | 3 |
| reference error | 154 | 10 (6.5%) | 143 | 1 |
| multiple error | 516 | 430 (83.3%) | 85 | 1 |

## Fix (2 changes)
### 1. compress_exception_only() — L96-104
```python
# Before:
def compress_exception_only(compressor, trace_events):
    parts = compressor._extract_exceptions(trace_events)
    if not parts:
        return EMPTY_MESSAGES["exception_only"]
    return "\n".join(parts)

# After:
def compress_exception_only(compressor, trace_events, test_results=None):
    parts = compressor._extract_exceptions(trace_events)
    if not parts and test_results and test_results.get("error"):
        parts = [f'[ERROR] {test_results["error"]}']
    if not parts:
        return EMPTY_MESSAGES["exception_only"]
    return "\n".join(parts)
```

### 2. format_sample() — L127-129
```python
# Before:
if condition == "exception_only":
    trace_text = compress_exception_only(compressor, trace_raw) if trace_raw else EMPTY_MESSAGES["exception_only"]

# After:
if condition == "exception_only":
    test_results = item.get("test_results", {})
    trace_text = compress_exception_only(compressor, trace_raw, test_results)
```

The two models differ primarily in pretraining data volume (5.5T vs.\ 2T tokens), providing a natural axis for evaluating whether trace signal utility is model-dependent \citep{dong2024composition}.

\subsection{Training Setup}

All conditions use identical training configurations to ensure fair comparison.
We apply LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) to all linear layers and train for 3 epochs with batch size 4, gradient accumulation 8 (effective batch size 32), learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup and linear decay, warmup ratio 0.1, and weight decay 0.01.
The maximum sequence length is 2,048 tokens; input sequences exceeding this limit are truncated from the input content while preserving the complete verdict label.
Training wall-clock time ranges from 0.5 to 2.5 hours per condition on a single GPU, depending on trace format verbosity.
The primary seed is 42; seed robustness is evaluated with seeds 123 and 456 for the \texttt{exception\_only} condition.

\subsection{Loss Ablation}

To disentangle training signal quality from input signal quality, we introduce a \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} variant.
This condition uses the same full trace as input but computes loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace tokens during training (loss weight = 0 on trace positions).
